pitchCorridor.what: Mound-to-plate flight time, and how it scales with the pitcher's arm.
pitchCorridor.whyThisRecordExists: src/config.ts's PITCH_SPEED block calls itself 'Backyard-measured' and states a ~250ms-to-~700ms corridor. Until 2026-07-24 NO record backed that claim -- it rests on two n=1 readings off the superseded YouTube stream. An in-code comment asserting a measurement that nothing gates is precisely the failure this file exists to prevent, so the claim now has a record even though the answer is still 'not measured'. conformance.test.js enforces the link.
pitchCorridor.whyWithdrawn: Filed 2026-07-25 as conformed/driftPct 0.0 on n=3 hand marks; withdrawn 2026-07-25 after review. Four independent problems, any one of which is disqualifying. (1) THE RELEASE FRAME IS NOT OBSERVABLE FOR THE PITCH TYPE MEASURED. The method's own classification rule is 'a fastball is invisible until late'; you cannot both identify a pitch as a laser BECAUSE the ball is not drawn early and claim to have read the frame it separated from the pitcher. CORRECTED 2026-07-26: an earlier draft of this record said the ball sprite is 'drawn in only ~5 frames'. That was wrong, and wrong the same way -- at low magnification BB's ~5px ball is LOST IN THE GRASS for the first two-thirds of its flight, but it IS drawn from release. Re-read at >=2x magnification the ball is visible leaving the hand. So 'release' was marked at the first frame the ball could be SPOTTED, which is late by construction -- the conclusion stands, the stated evidence did not. (2) THE TARGET SHADOW WAS NOT DISTINGUISHED FROM THE BALL. BB draws a descending target indicator on the corridor floor. It is smooth, monotone and reads exactly like a ball track. instrument.backgroundSubtraction records a ~930ms descent being rejected as 'a shadow'; that object is the target indicator, its span is ~3.5x the recorded flight, and which of the two bounds the flight was never settled. (3) PRECISION EXCEEDS THE SOURCE. instrument.frameRate sets effectiveFramePeriodMs 50 for session2 and warns a ~250ms flight is +-20%% needing n>=5; the corridor was read off a 33ms sheet at n=3 and every value is a round multiple of 10ms. fastballSpread 50 is exactly one frame period, i.e. the tolerance was the noise. (4) THE SAME PITCH IS RECORDED FOUR WAYS. t=53.90 appears as 220ms (capture index), 233ms (this record's own bracket), 234ms (instrument.clockValidity) and 250ms (the sample's ms). clockValidity also records a 100ms gap between last-seen-in-hand and first-seen-airborne -- a +-43%% ambiguity on the start endpoint of a ~230ms quantity, never propagated here.

supersedes.why: The conformance was to a number whose start endpoint the method could not observe. Recorded rather than deleted: this file exists so a withdrawn measurement leaves a trail.
supersedes.coupledChanges: Matching the flight FORCED other constants, all recorded because none of them is measured: (1) the swing windows had to shrink -- a 380ms CONTACT band against a 270ms flight means a tap at the instant of release still connects, so timing would stop being a skill. Scaled by the same 0.371 (see pace.swingWindows). (2) PITCH_SPEED.LOB.FROM_MS 850 -> 315, or nothing would ever lob again (the slowest possible pitch is now 675ms) and the rainbow-arc readability cue would have silently died. At 315 the fastball stays flat and off-speed arcs -- BB's own laser-vs-lob split. (3) kid PITCH_TRAVEL_MS and CPU_PITCH_TRAVEL_MS scaled likewise; TEE_PITCH_MS deliberately untouched as the accessibility escape hatch.
supersedes.retuneCoherenceNote: The 2026-07-24 pace retune scaled the live-play sim 1.987x and did NOT touch PITCH_SPEED, so the pitch became ~2x faster RELATIVE to everything around it. That is real, and it is not why pitching feels fast -- see pace.pitchCadence, which is the actual finding.
supersedes.conformNote: RETUNED 2026-07-25. MAIN_BASE_MS 800 -> 297 puts an average arm at exactly BB's measured 270ms, and our 203-324ms range brackets BB's measured lasers (250/270/290). We were 2.7x slower, with our FASTEST pitch slower than BB's SLOWEST measured one.
supersedes.withdrawnMethod: Pitches located by the HUD count pips (instrument.pip-pitch-index), then each read frame-by-frame off a 33ms corridor sheet (crop native x245-410, y88-363; 24 tiles, cols 8). Release = the frame the ball separates from the pitcher; arrival = the frame it is inside the yellow strike-zone bracket. Classified LASER vs LOB by the documented tell: a fastball is invisible until late and flat, off-speed is visible from release. The split is cleanly bimodal (250/270/290 vs 420/430/480), which is what makes the classification trustworthy.
supersedes.whatTheyActuallyBound: Kept for the trail, and because they are a clean worked example of the error. Each is the tail of a flight -- the stretch where the sprite was big enough to spot -- not release-to-plate. Their MEDIAN (270ms) is ~22% of the stopwatch-gated 1230ms, which is about what you get if you catch only the last third of an accelerating approach. Note the laser:lob RATIO of 1.7x survived the error; only the absolutes did not.

umpCallDelay.whatWouldWork: The pitches are now located (see pace.betweenPitch.method and the pip technique in instrument.pipPitchIndex). One 33ms sheet per pitch resolves it; n>=6 is reachable.

partialReading.method: Read off the same mound-to-plate sheets as pace.betweenPitch: ball arrival -> the BALL!/STRIKE! starburst appearing.
partialReading.why: NOT promoted despite n=4. The sheets step at 250ms and the quantity is ~200ms, so the sampling interval is the SAME ORDER as the thing being measured: this cannot tell our 200ms from BB's 250ms, and reporting a median of 250 would claim a resolution the read does not have. The honest statement is 'roughly 150-250ms, consistent with our 200ms'. A 33ms sheet over these same, now-known pitch times would settle it cheaply.

flyHang.what: Deep-fly hang time, as a RATIO to the home->1B anchor. The ratio is the durable form: absolute hang times cannot be compared across two games with different field scales.

priorReading.why: One sample, off a stream whose timestamps no longer locate it, and it is now contradicted: it claimed a ratio of 0.667 where the measured range is 0.685-1.208.

flyHang.definition: Contact -> the ball is caught or first touches the ground. Contact is free and exact: it is the findCuts cut time, because BB cuts to the wide view on the frame of contact.
flyHang.confidenceNote: Derived 'low' because relative spread is 0.65, and that is the RIGHT arithmetic applied to the wrong shape of quantity: FLY_HANG_MS is a MIN/MAX RANGE, so the spread here is the signal (a shallow fly against a deep one), not measurement error. Each individual sample is pinned to +-50ms -- 1.4% at 3.6s -- because all four were read frame by frame off zoomed sheets. Not hand-raised: confidence() stays derived, and the caveat is recorded instead.
flyHang.method: BB's LANDING-PREVIEW DISC, not the ball. See instrument.landing-disc for why the ball itself is not trackable here. The disc appears on the frame of contact and vanishes on the frame the flight ends -- verified by eye on all four samples, including one where the ball LANDS rather than being caught, so the disc marks end-of-flight either way.
excluded: play-09 (5383ms) and play-18 (5417ms) are HOME RUNS. Their discs are real and both read ~5.4s, but a ball that leaves the park is not what LIVE.LAUNCH.FLY_HANG_MS models -- our sim decides homers at launch and they never enter the live-play hang. Recorded here rather than silently dropped, and worth noting they are longer than every in-play sample.
play-08 and play-14 draw no landing disc at all. play-14 is an infield pop that BB banners as INFIELD FLY; the disc appears to be an outfield affordance.
flyHang.driftNote: Our flies DO hang long relative to the run, but by 14-38% -- not the 42-106% the superseded n=1 reading implied. And the absolute direction is the opposite of what everyone assumed: BB's flies hang 2.9-5.1s against our 2.0-2.9s, i.e. LONGER than ours. The defect was never that our flies are slow; it is that our RUN is fast.
flyHang.retuneWarning: Fixing LIVE.RUNNER_SPEED alone OVERSHOOTS. At a 4200ms anchor our current 2000-2900ms flies would sit at ratios 0.476-0.690 against BB's 0.685-1.208 -- too SHORT at both ends. To match BB, FLY_HANG_MS has to go UP to about {MIN: 2875, MAX: 5075} at the same time. Note also that BB's range is WIDER than ours (a 1.76x span against our 1.45x), so shallow and deep flies are more different from each other than we make them.
flyHang.conformNote: RETUNED 2026-07-24 to BB's measured range. Note the direction: FLY_HANG_MS went UP (2000-2900 -> 2875-5075), because the long-assumed 'our flies hang too long' defect was really 'our run is too fast'. Fixing RUNNER_SPEED alone would have left flies too SHORT -- the retuneWarning below is what that trap was.

betweenPitch.definition: Ball ARRIVES at the plate -> the PITCHER HAS IT BACK and is ready to throw again. That is the forced beat FLOW.BETWEEN_PITCH_MS models. What follows it in BB is player deliberation over the swing cards, which is not a game constant and is excluded.
betweenPitch.method: Pitches LOCATED by the HUD count pips (a resolved pitch lights one; nothing else does -- mound motion is also produced by the pitcher's idle ball-toss), then each cycle read by eye off a 20-tile mound-to-plate sheet at 250ms. The full beat is visible in one sheet: ball arrives -> call banner -> ball rests at its crossing spot -> catcher returns it -> pitcher has it.
betweenPitch.sampleGranularity: Read at 250ms steps, so each sample carries +-125ms -- 5% of a 2550ms quantity. Fine here; NOT fine for pace.umpCallDelay, which is why that one stays unmeasured.
betweenPitch.driftNote: Ours is 1250ms against BB's 2550ms -- we are 51% fast, almost exactly the 50% the anchor is fast. AND THE RATIO IS ALREADY RIGHT: as a fraction of the home->1B anchor, BB is 0.607 and we are 0.591, a 2.7% difference. So this constant is correctly PROPORTIONED and only wrong in absolute tempo -- unlike fly hang, which is wrong in both. Scaling it by the same factor as RUNNER_SPEED lands it within a few percent of BB with no separate judgement call.
betweenPitch.conformNote: RETUNED 2026-07-24. Was already correctly PROPORTIONED (0.591 vs 0.607) and wrong only in absolute tempo, so it moved with the anchor and now matches outright.

pitchCadence.what: How long the game waits before throwing the next pitch AT the player -- the beat that decides how rushed batting feels.

ours.behaviour: the MOUND idle clock: when the human is pitching and never picks a pitch, the game picks a fastball down the middle for them. Batting is not gated on input at all -- the pitch fires on FLOW.BETWEEN_PITCH_MS, with PLATE_VIEW.CEREMONY animating that wait and any tap skipping it.

pitchCadence.informs: src/config.ts FLOW.BETWEEN_PITCH_MS, PLATE_VIEW.CEREMONY, and the GameScene pitch scheduling

supersedes.was: BB DOES NOT USE A TIMER.
supersedes.why: OVERCLAIM, corrected on the player's report. The footage only showed that the observed gaps (10.7 / 11.6 / 19.5s) never REACHED a clock -- not that none exists. Seth, who has played the game, reports there IS a pitch clock, just long enough that normal play never hits it. Absence of evidence was written up as evidence of absence; the corrected claim is the one the footage actually supports.
supersedes.lesson: A measurement can only bound what it observed. 'No gap reached X' does not license 'there is no X'.

supersedes.was: The clock is a BATTING-side backstop: BB waits for the batter to choose a swing, so we gate the pitch on a swing-card tap.
supersedes.why: WRONG MECHANISM, corrected on the player's report. The long gaps are real, but they are not BB waiting for a swing selection -- they are the between-pitch CEREMONY (catcher throws back, pitcher gets set) playing out, which is skippable, and Seth was skipping it. The clock he was describing is on the PITCHING side. The numbers in `measured` were never wrong; the story told about what produced them was, and the gate built on that story shipped in #24 and is reverted here.
supersedes.lesson: A gap is a duration, not an explanation. Timing footage bounds HOW LONG a beat lasts and says nothing about WHAT fills it -- and an inferred mechanism dressed as a measured one is the more dangerous error, because it inherits the measurement's credibility.

pitchCadence.conformNote: RETUNED 2026-07-25, then re-scoped the same day. The clock now guards only the mound (beginPitchTurn's auto-pick); nothing on the batting side waits for input, so no mode can hang on a tap that never comes. The worst-case mound turn (clock + PITCH_METER_MS + PITCH_AUTO_THROW_MS = 11.9s) stays under NET.ACTION_TIMEOUT_MS, which launchPitchMain's netWaitFor depends on for liveness.

swingWindows.what: The swing timing windows, and why they can never be measured from BB footage.
swingWindows.finding: A timing window is an INTERNAL TOLERANCE -- how many ms of error still makes contact -- with no on-screen representation. No amount of video reveals BB's, because you would need the player's exact tap times, which no recording captures. So unlike the flight time, this constant has to be CHOSEN.
swingWindows.whatForcedIt: Matching BB's 270ms fastball made the old windows structurally broken, not merely mistuned: CONTACT was 380ms, wider than the entire flight, so an errorMs of -270 (a tap at the instant of release) sat inside the band and contact was guaranteed. Verified against the real code path -- bandFromError compares Math.abs(errorMs) to absolute-ms constants and never references travelMs.
swingWindows.choice: Scaled by exactly the factor the flight scaled (0.371), so every internal relationship is unchanged: window as a fraction of flight, and the SWING_TYPES deltas relative to the windows. main 120/240/380 -> 45/89/141; kid 80/170/300 -> 30/63/111; SWING_TYPES SAFE 60->22, BIG 45->17, BUNT 80->30, CRAZY_BUNT 100->37.
swingWindows.caveat: This preserves the RATIO, not the absolute difficulty. Human timing jitter is absolute (~50-100ms), so a 30ms PERFECT band is genuinely harder to hit than an 80ms one -- batting IS harder now, and a 270ms flight rewards anticipation over reaction, which is what BB does too. These are the first dial to widen if it plays badly. TEE_PITCH_MS (1500, untouched) is the escape hatch for the youngest players.
swingWindows.structuralInvariant: CONTACT must stay below the FASTEST possible travelMs in every mode, or timing becomes free again. Asserted in conformance.test.js.

pitchWindup.what: How long BB2001's pitcher takes from his first delivery motion to releasing the ball.

simClock.what: Why every pace.* record is allowed to be an absolute real-millisecond claim, and what would silently make them all wrong.
simClock.theClaim: GameScene steps the live sim on Phaser's raw frame delta, so one sim-millisecond IS one real-millisecond. That is the only reason a constant in config.ts can be compared against a stopwatch reading off BB2001 -- pace.homeToFirst's 4197ms, pace.flyHang's 2875-5075, all of it.
simClock.theTrap: conformance.test.js's ourHomeToFirstMs passes `tempo: 1` as a LITERAL, and was commented as though that defended the claim: 'introducing a tempo dial later breaks HERE, loudly, instead of silently invalidating every ratio in measures.json'. It does not. A tempo scalar changes what the game DOES and changes nothing the test COMPUTES.
simClock.theEvidence: PR #17 (Split action tempo into TEMPO and PITCH_TEMPO, opened 2026-07-23, closed 2026-07-28) was test-merged into main on 2026-07-28. With TEMPO 0.6 the real home->1B becomes 6995ms against BB's measured 4200 -- 66% too slow -- while pace.homeToFirst went on reporting 4197 and conformed. Fly hang became 4792-8458 real. All 449 tests passed.
simClock.whyItWasTemptingAndWrong: PR #17's premise was correct when written: home->1B ran ~2.1s. The 2026-07-24 pace retune fixed that at the source by moving LIVE.RUNNER_SPEED to 42.8 px/s. A tempo scalar landing afterwards applies the same correction a second time.

Three checks, each verified to FAIL against PR #17's actual diff before being committed: config.ts exports no *TEMPO* constant; stepLivePlay's dt argument is the bare identifier `delta` (scoped to that call -- the replay's FX.REPLAY.SPEED playback clock legitimately scales delta and never reaches the sim); and getPitchBaseMs's body contains no arithmetic at all, checked structurally rather than by variable name.

What this forbids is adding one INVISIBLY. Teach the conformance records to derive the tempo instead of hardcoding 1, then delete the lint in the same commit, with the reasoning attached.

sim.note: The v2 SIM's constants. A new reference class: these answer to PUBLISHED PHYSICS and to real baseball, not to BB2001 footage -- which is why every record carries `reference`, and why that field became required in the same change. Conforming a game for four-to-eight-year-olds to MLB's strikeout rate is the mistake that field exists to prevent.

ballPhysics.what: The ball and the air it flies through, folded into the single factor the aerodynamic model needs: K = 1/2 * rho * A / m.
ballPhysics.why: K is the validation, not just a convenience. It combines air density, cross-sectional area and mass, so deriving it from the four published constants and comparing against Nathan's INDEPENDENTLY published figure exercises all three at once. That is a better check than terminal velocity, which the plan originally called for: terminal velocity is only ever as good as the C_D you assume, and C_D is the least certain input here.
ballPhysics.theGap: 0.29%, and it is NATHAN'S ROUNDING rather than our arithmetic. His Eq. 9 normalises on 'the density of air is nominally 1.225 kg/m^3 (or 0.0767 lb/ft^3)', but 1.225 kg/m^3 is really 0.076482 lb/ft^3. Feeding his rounded 0.0767 into our own formula reproduces 5.509e-3 exactly, which is what proves the difference is bookkeeping. Recorded rather than reconciled: adopting a rounded density to make two numbers agree is fitting the constant to the citation.
ballPhysics.nNote: n=1 is the right number for a published constant. This is a rulebook and a standard atmosphere, not a sample.
ballPhysics.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/flight.test.ts 'derives K from the published constants and lands on Nathan figure', which also reproduces his value from his own rounded density.

aeroModel.what: Drag and Magnus lift, taken verbatim from Nathan's Trajectory Calculator fit rather than invented.
aeroModel.model: C_D = C_D0 + C_D1*(omega/1000rpm), with C_D0 0.297 and C_D1 0.0292. C_L = C_L2*S/(C_L0 + C_L1*S), with C_L0 0.583, C_L1 2.333, C_L2 1.120, and S = R*omega/v.
aeroModel.theHappyConsequence: BOTH FORMS ARE PURE ARITHMETIC. The plan assumed the coefficients would need committed interpolation tables, because ECMAScript specifies Math.exp/log/pow and the trig functions as implementation-approximated while only + - * / and Math.sqrt are correctly rounded -- so a determinism fingerprint built on them goes red on a V8 bump and reads as somebody's bug. Nathan's fit needs none of them. The whole aerodynamic model is bit-stable with no tables at all, and purity.lint.test.js now enforces that the per-step path stays that way.

validation.conditions: 100 mph exit velocity, 30 deg launch angle, 3 ft contact height.
validation.against: The Statcast rule of thumb that a well-struck ball (100mph/30deg) carries about 400 ft. Backspin must also carry FURTHER than no spin and topspin SHORTER, asserted separately.

aeroModel.caveat: THE FIT IS NOT FOR OUR REGIME, and that is recorded rather than glossed. It comes from MLB fly balls with exit velocity >= 90 mph and launch angles 20-35 deg, measured indoors at Tropicana Field (Nathan estimates rho = 1.194 there), and he verifies C_D's velocity-independence only 'at least for speeds in the range 60-110 mph'. Our batters hit 35-50 mph. Everything below 60 mph is an unvalidated extrapolation. The model is conformed on what was published; the extrapolation is not, and sim.aeroModelLowSpeed is where that gets closed.
aeroModel.nNote: n=1 for a published fit: the sample is Nathan's, not ours.
aeroModel.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/flight.test.ts -- the coefficient forms, the saturating C_L bound, drag's independence from speed, and the MLB carry band.

aeroModelLowSpeed.what: Whether Nathan's drag fit still holds at the 35-60 mph exit velocities a four-to-eight-year-old actually produces.
aeroModelLowSpeed.why: His stated result is that after accounting for spin there is 'no further dependence on v, at least for speeds in the range 60-110 mph'. Every ball this game cares most about is below that band. The model may well hold -- Reynolds number falls with speed and the drag crisis is at the other end -- but nobody has said so, and the point of this file is that unmeasured things stay enumerable instead of becoming folklore.

ours.value: Nathan's fit, extrapolated below its verified band.

aeroModelLowSpeed.significanceRaisedBy: PR 4 (2026-07-31). This was written as a caveat on an otherwise-conformed model, worth recording but not urgent. The power-to-bat-speed mapping has now made it the single most load-bearing open question in the sim: the roster's exit velocities run 43.5-61.4 mph, so TWENTY-NINE OF THIRTY KIDS produce batted balls below the 60 mph floor of the band Nathan's drag fit was verified over. Essentially every ball this game will ever simulate is an extrapolation past the edge of the measurement. The model may well hold there -- Reynolds number falls with speed and the drag crisis is at the other end -- but nothing has said so, and the statistical harness in PR 8 will be measuring BABIP against a drag law nobody has checked in the regime it runs in.
aeroModelLowSpeed.whatWouldWork: Either a published low-speed C_D measurement for a real baseball (Kensrud & Smith, 'In situ drag measurements of sports balls', Procedia Engineering 13 (2011), covers a wider speed range and is the first place to look), or a direct one: launch a ball at a measured speed and angle with known spin, film it against a scale, and fit C_D from the trajectory. n>=3 per speed bin.

integratorStep.what: What FLIGHT_HZ is actually for, measured rather than inherited from the design doc.
integratorStep.theFinding: NOT ACCURACY. docs/OVERVIEW.md promised 'integrated RK4 at 240Hz' before any integrator existed, and the natural assumption is that 240 was an accuracy figure. It is not: RK4 here is fourth order (measured error ratios 16.20 and 16.13 per halving of the step, against a textbook 2^4 = 16), and ACCURACY IS SATURATED BY 60 Hz -- a 60 Hz flight lands within 3e-9 ft of a 15360 Hz one, and 240 Hz within 6e-12 ft. Nothing in this game can see 3e-9 ft.
integratorStep.whatItIsFor: Two things, both real. (1) PHASE: 240 = 4x60 = 2x120, so at both common refresh rates the fixed-timestep accumulator's remainder is exactly zero and the renderer's interpolation alpha is exact. (2) COLLISION SAMPLING: guards are evaluated once per step, so the step size bounds how briefly a condition can hold and still be noticed. Bisection makes a DETECTED crossing exact; it cannot detect one that opens and closes inside a single step.

measured.method: The same launch integrated at each rate; error is the carry difference against a 15360 Hz reference.

integratorStep.theTestTrap: The first version of the convergence test compared 240/480/960 Hz and got a ratio of ZERO, which read as a broken integrator. At those rates the discretisation error is already at the double-precision floor, so the ratio was measuring rounding. A convergence test has to run COARSE to measure convergence -- the same class of error as pace.pitchCorridor's 'the tolerance was the noise'.
integratorStep.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/flight.test.ts -- fourth-order convergence on a clean flight AND through a bounce (the second is what catches an event handler that bisects and then Euler-steps the remainder, which every clean-flight test passes while the global order silently drops to one), plus the phase divisibility.

carryVsFence.what: How much exit velocity it takes to clear each venue's fence, against how hard a four-to-eight-year-old can actually hit a ball.
carryVsFence.why: This was the v2 plan's ranked #1 risk, written as 'every ball is a home run' -- MLB-shaped exit velocities over a 200ft park. The truth is the MIRROR IMAGE, and the integrator alone was enough to find it, before any contact model, fielder or play reducer existed that could have absorbed a wrong answer by being tuned around it.

carryVsFence.theProblem: Published youth guidance puts 8-and-under exit velocity at 45-55 mph off a TEE, with game exit velocity 5-10 mph lower -- so a real 4-8-year-old hits 35-50 mph and clears NOTHING. The park's shortest fence needs 57.5 mph and its centre field needs 62.5.

PR 4 maps power 1-10 onto roughly 35-60 mph exit velocity, so only genuine sluggers clear the short parts, the park's 212ft centre stays out of reach for everyone, and the sandlot's 150ft porch becomes the cheap-homer park its own data file already intends. That costs no geometry change, makes `power` legible on the field, and makes the draft matter -- which is the product.

A deep outfield a gap ball can land in is the entire reason v2 exists -- v1 had 1.49 basepaths and 0% BABIP.

flyHangRatio.what: Kid-scale fly-ball hang time as a RATIO to the home-to-first anchor -- the one place real RK4 physics can be checked against a measurement this project made itself.
flyHangRatio.why: Absolute hang times cannot be compared across two games with different field scales, which is why pace.flyHang recorded a ratio in the first place. That makes it the only BB2001 measurement transferring to v2 unchanged: no pixels, no new capture, and it checks EMERGENT physics rather than a constant somebody typed.
flyHangRatio.verdict: Kid-scale flies land at the LOW end of BB's measured band, and the shallowest fall below it. That is the expected direction -- a 45 mph pop-up cannot hang like a 95 mph one -- and the deep flies that matter for defensive play (EV 55-60) sit inside it. Recorded as conformed on the deep-fly cases with the shallow ones stated, rather than claiming the whole range.
flyHangRatio.nNote: The BB band's n=4 and low confidence are inherited from pace.flyHang; this record cannot be more confident than the anchor it is measured against.

bounceModel.what: The FORM of a ground impact: normal restitution, plus a tangential grip/slip branch that couples the ball's spin to its forward speed.
bounceModel.model: Normal: vy' = -e*vy. Tangential: the contact point's horizontal velocity is u = v_t + w x (-R*yhat). Gripping it costs an impulse of (2/7)*m*|u|; Coulomb friction can supply mu*m*(1+e)*|vy|. If it can afford it the contact point stops (GRIP), giving v' = (5v - 2wR)/7; otherwise the full friction impulse is applied opposing the slip (SLIP). Spin updates from the same impulse in both branches.
bounceModel.whyConformed: The form is DERIVABLE, and was derived rather than recalled: solving the impulse problem for a sphere (I = 2/5 mR^2, contact one radius below the centre) with the rolling-contact condition gives J = -(2/7)m(v + wR) directly. Verified three ways in bounce.test.ts -- pure rolling in gives zero impulse, an unspun ball gives exactly 5/7, and angular momentum about the contact point is conserved in BOTH branches, which is the property the 2/7 is a consequence of rather than an assumption alongside.
bounceModel.theSign: v' = (5v - 2wR)/7. The MINUS is the part memory gets wrong, and getting it wrong makes backspin behave like topspin. Its consequence is checked directly: forward speed falls monotonically with backspin, is roughly halved at a realistic 200 rad/s (1910 rpm), and reverses only between 300 and 800 rad/s -- 2900 to 7600 rpm, off the top of the real batted-ball range. The headline 'backspin bounces the ball BACKWARD' is true of the model and NOT true of a baseball, and the record says so rather than repeating the catchier version.
bounceModel.emergentAndCorrect: TOPSPIN ACCELERATES THE BALL off the bounce -- measured here at 12.21 -> 12.92 ft/s -- because friction converts rotational energy into translational. Total energy still falls (191.7 -> 111.9). The first version of the test asserted that speed never increases, failed on exactly this case, and looked like a bug when it was the physics being right. The invariant is ENERGY, and the acceleration is now asserted directly so nobody re-caps it.
bounceModel.knownSimplification: Cross (2002) measured that real balls GRIP rather than roll, with the friction force reversing mid-bounce and the spin exceeding the rolling prediction. Our grip branch is the idealised limit, so it under-predicts spin reversal. Sidespin-induced lateral deflection is also unmodelled: the impulse is applied in the plane of the slip, and spin about the vertical is left untouched.
bounceModel.nNote: n=1 for a derivation. It is checked by conserved quantities, not by sampling.
bounceModel.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/bounce.test.ts 'the ground bounce' -- contact point at rest after a grip, exactly 5/7 unspun, rolling-in-stays-rolling, angular momentum conserved across both branches, slip when the impact is too glancing, and energy never increasing on a full sweep of every venue.

groundBounce.what: The ground coefficient of restitution for each venue's surface -- the COEFFICIENT, where sim.bounceModel is the form.

partialReading.source: Brosnan & McNitt's Pennbounce work at Penn State's Center for Sports Surface Research.
partialReading.theCheckItAlreadyBuys: At COR_BASE 0.50 the venue multipliers that were hand-authored MONTHS BEFORE this band was found land at park 0.50 and sandlot 0.40 -- both inside it -- while the blacktop's 0.65 falls outside, correctly, because asphalt is not a turf surface and the band is for infields. A cross-check of somebody else's guesswork against real literature, and it held.
partialReading.why: Read from a secondary summary of the primary papers rather than the papers themselves, and the band covers infield surfaces rather than the mown outfield grass, shaggy backyard lawn and asphalt this game actually has. n=1 source, not n=1 measurement.

groundBounce.whatWouldWork: Read Brosnan & McNitt directly for the per-surface figures; or measure it, which is genuinely cheap: drop a baseball from a measured height onto mown grass, shaggy grass and asphalt, film against a scale, and take COR = sqrt(rebound height / drop height). n>=3 per surface.

rollFriction.what: The rolling friction coefficient per surface, which sets how far a grounder travels once it stops bouncing.
rollFriction.why: field.ts authors 0.28 (mown grass), 0.36 (shaggy backyard grass) and 0.10 (asphalt) with a comment and no citation. They are now load-bearing: a ball rolling at v covers exactly v^2/(2*mu*g), so mu IS the roll distance.
rollFriction.whatWouldWork: Roll a baseball from a measured initial speed across each surface and time it to a stop, then invert the closed form: mu = v^2 / (2*g*d). A phone camera and a tape measure are enough. n>=3 per surface. The ORDERING is not in doubt (asphalt < mown grass < shaggy grass); the magnitudes are.

wallRestitution.what: The coefficient of restitution off each venue's outfield wall, and how much tangential speed a carom keeps.
wallRestitution.why: A ball off the wall is a double, so this decides how often the deepest hits pay. The Pennbounce band does NOT apply -- it is for GROUND surfaces, and a painted wall, wooden planks and chain-link are three different problems.
wallRestitution.whatWouldWork: Throw a ball at a measured speed square into each wall type and film the rebound; COR is the speed ratio. The tangential figure needs an oblique throw and two angles measured. n>=3 each. Chain-link is the interesting one -- it is a net, not a wall, and may not behave like a restitution at all.

venueRollFeel.what: Which venue plays FAST, once bounce and roll are both simulated -- and the answer contradicts what the venues were authored to be.
venueRollFeel.theFinding: THE BLACKTOP PLAYS SHORTEST. It has by far the lowest rolling friction (0.10 against 0.28 and 0.36), and in isolation a ball rolling on it travels 3.6x as far. But end to end a batted ball comes to rest SHORTEST there, because its restitution is also the highest (0.65): the ball spends its energy BOUNCING rather than rolling -- 6 or 7 hops against 3 or 4 -- and every landing takes tangential speed out through the grip. A surface cannot be both the springiest and the fastest.

measured.conditions: EV 70mph, launch angle 8 deg, spray -20, 1200 rpm, contact 2.5ft.
measured.isolatedRollRatio: asphalt rolls 3.6x as far as shaggy grass from the same entry speed -- the friction model is doing exactly what it should.

drift.note: The sandlot's shaggy grass -- the surface authored to be the DEADEST -- carries a ball nearly twice as far as the asphalt authored to be the fastest.

venueRollFeel.theIntent: data/venues.ts calls the blacktop 'hot asphalt -- the ball SPRINGS' and gives it rollMult 1.3, i.e. the fast park; the sandlot gets 'dead hops off the lumpy lawn'. v1 could hold both because its bounceMult and rollMult were independent renderer-domain knobs with no physics between them. Real physics couples them.
venueRollFeel.whyNotJustRetune: Because that would be tuning a constant to make a test pass, which is the failure mode this whole file exists to catch. The blacktop's high restitution is the CORRECT reading of a hard surface -- Pennbounce found COR tracks surface hardness directly. What is wrong is the expectation that hard also means fast.
venueRollFeel.whatWouldClose: A venue-feel pass in the retune PR, with the choice made explicitly: either accept that the blacktop is a high-hop park and change its description, or lower bounceMult and accept a less springy asphalt. Both are legitimate; picking one quietly is not.
venueRollFeel.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/bounce.test.ts 'plays SHORTEST on the blacktop', which pins the drift ratio between 1.5 and 2.5 so it can neither grow nor be half-fixed unnoticed.

batBallCollision.what: How a swing becomes an exit velocity: Nathan's collision-efficiency identity, and the recoil factor that makes a youth bat different from an adult's.
batBallCollision.model: v_f = e_A*v_ball + (1 + e_A)*v_bat (Eq. 3), with e_A = (e - r)/(1 + r) and r = m/M_eff (Eqs. 6-7).
batBallCollision.whyConformed: Eq. 3 is an IDENTITY, not a fit -- exact for any ball, bat and collision model -- so it is asserted symbolically over a grid of inputs rather than in a band. e_A is not stated either: it is recomputed from the ball-bat COR and the bat's effective mass, so EFFECTIVE_MASS_OZ and e_A cannot drift apart.
batBallCollision.theKidResult: At a youth bat's ~14oz effective mass, e_A = 0.098 against an adult's ~0.20 at 20.5oz. The recoil factor is the entire mechanism -- no fudge factor appears anywhere -- and it is monotone in bat mass, which the test sweeps.
batBallCollision.independentCheck: Off a TEE the pitch contributes nothing, so v_f = (1 + e_A)*v_bat with no free parameter at all. At e_A 0.098, bat speeds of 40-50 mph give 44-55 mph, against a published 8-and-under tee band of 45-55. Two unrelated sources -- a physics identity and coaching benchmarks -- agreeing.
batBallCollision.nNote: n=1 for a published identity. It is checked by symbolic exactness, not by sampling.
batBallCollision.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/contact.test.ts 'the collision' -- Eq. 3 as an identity over a grid, e_A recomputed from Eq. 6, monotonicity in bat mass, and the tee-band cross-check.

obliqueContact.what: How the undercut sets launch angle and backspin -- the same grip/slip result the ground bounce uses, one collision later.
obliqueContact.model: The barrel's centre passing `undercut` below the ball's tilts the line of centres by asin(undercut/(r_ball + r_barrel)); the ball leaves along it. The tangential component at that contact is gripped, giving spin (5/7)*v_t/R, exactly as sim.bounceModel derives for the ground.
obliqueContact.theEnhancementIsNotApplied: ★ Kensrud, Nathan & Smith measured spin 'up to 40% greater than would be obtained by rolling contact of rigid bodies', and applying that 1.4 DOUBLE-COUNTS. Working their numbers back: they measured 0-3500 rpm over 0-30 deg at 63-88 mph, and the rigid-body rolling prediction at 30 deg and 88 mph is ALREADY ~3600 rpm. Their ceiling sits at the rolling limit, not 40% above it, so the 40% is normalised against something the abstract does not state. Multiplying our rolling result by 1.4 put a kid's batted ball at 4600-5400 rpm, outside the band the paper measured. We use the derived rolling limit, which lands inside it.

validation.note: Our model reaches 3622 rpm at a 32 deg launch -- outside the ANGLE range they measured, so the test deliberately restricts its sweep to <=30 deg rather than comparing an extrapolation against a band that never covered it.
validation.linearity: Both of Kensrud's stated linearities are asserted: exit speed and spin each scale linearly with bat speed.

obliqueContact.nNote: n=1 for a derivation checked against one published experiment.
obliqueContact.whatWouldClose: Read Kensrud et al. in full for the normalisation behind the 40% figure. If it is against a reference model rather than the plain rolling limit, GRIP_SPIN_ENHANCEMENT can be set honestly instead of left at 1.
obliqueContact.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/contact.test.ts 'the batted ball' -- undercut lifts and backspins, topping chops and puts topspin on, spin stays in the measured band inside the measured angle range, and both linearities.

batSpeed.what: The map from the 1-10 `power` stat to a real bat speed -- the one number that decides whether anybody in this game can hit a home run.
batSpeed.why: ★ THE FIRST RECORD TO USE reference: 'baseball'. The vocabulary has carried that value since it was introduced and nothing had ever needed it: this is neither BB2001 footage, nor published physics, nor arithmetic off our own constants. It is what real children actually do, which is a fourth kind of claim.

partialReading.source: Coaching benchmarks and swing-sensor aggregates (WIN Reality, Blast Motion, >7,000 lessons).
partialReading.why: Coaching benchmarks rather than a dataset, and they START at 9U -- our players are four to eight, BELOW the floor. Our 35-53 band is that data extrapolated DOWN, which is exactly the kind of move this file exists to keep visible.
partialReading.boxedInFromTheOtherSide: The top of the band is not free either: sim.carryVsFence requires that a power-10 kid clear the park's 185ft line and that NOBODY clear its 212ft centre. Both constraints -- extrapolated coaching data from below, and the fence from above -- land on the same number, which is the only reason it is worth stating at all.

batSpeed.rosterNote: NOBODY ON THE ROSTER HAS POWER 1. The realised span is power 2 (Sprout, Noodle) to power 10 (Big Lou), so the mapping is defined over 1-10 but only ever evaluated over 2-10. Any claim about 'a power-1 kid' is about a kid who does not exist, and a test pins that.
batSpeed.whatWouldWork: Bat-sensor readings from three or more actual four-to-eight-year-olds. A Blast Motion or Diamond Kinetics knob sensor and an afternoon at a tee-ball practice would close it outright, and would replace an extrapolation with a measurement of exactly the population this game is for.

pitchCorridorV2.what: The pitch's flight time, and the release velocity solved from it.
pitchCorridorV2.theReparameterisation: ★ THE MEASURED QUANTITY IS A TIME, NOT A SPEED, and conflating them is a mistake this PR made first. pace.pitchCorridor brackets 1230ms over the 46ft mound, and docs/OVERVIEW.md summarises that as '25.6 mph -- exactly a seven-year-old's fastball'. That figure is 46ft/1.23s: the ball's average PACE toward the plate. Using it as a RELEASE SPEED puts the pitch 26 FEET UNDERGROUND at the plate, because a 46ft flight lasting 1.23s falls 24ft under gravity on the way. So the flight time is the anchor and the release velocity is SOLVED from it -- two constraints (cross at the aim height, take this long) determining two unknowns.

partialReading.why: Inherited verbatim from pace.pitchCorridor, whose own note reads: 'n=1 at this rigour. The repo convention is n<3 stays a partialReading, and the entire point of this record is that overclaiming is how the 270ms happened.' Consuming a number does not measure it.
partialReading.armIsUncalibrated: pace.pitchCorridor.armRatingCaveat: BB's on-screen 'PT' is a pitches-thrown counter rather than a rating, so flight time cannot be bound to a pitcher stat from that footage -- 'ARM_MULT remains uncalibrated'. Our arm spread is a spread around the one measured flight and is honest about being one.

pitchCorridorV2.theBreakIsEmergent: v1's pitchkind.ts does not fly a ball: it lerps a straight line and adds a bow forced to zero at BOTH ends, so the crossing point is a rolled endpoint rather than a consequence of the release. Here a curveball breaks because flight.ts applies the Magnus force to its spin. That surfaced a bug the aim solve HID: every spin axis was inverted, so the 'backspin' fastball sank and the curve rose while breaking toward FIRST -- and the pitch still arrived exactly on its aim point, because the solve compensated. Only the lateral break shows it, which is why a test asserts the break DIRECTION.
pitchCorridorV2.whatWouldWork: pace.pitchCorridor's own closing work, unchanged: ~6 more flights from the stopwatch-gated capture, classified by the on-screen pitch card, each read at >=2x magnification.

kidSprintSpeed.what: How fast a kid runs, and how long they take to get there -- one speed function that both a baserunner and a fielder call.
kidSprintSpeed.why: ★ THE ANCHOR IS ONE EQUATION IN TWO UNKNOWNS, and treating it as one is how a 'measured' constant gets invented. pace.homeToFirst measures 4200ms over a 60ft leg (n=3, spread 261, confidence med) and calls itself 'THE anchor: every other pace constant is measured against it'. But a leg time constrains a (top speed, acceleration) PAIR, not either one. v1 resolved that by assuming NO acceleration -- 60/4.2 = 14.286 ft/s flat, for every kid, from the frame of contact -- which is too fast out of the box and too slow at the bag, and which is also why defense.cpuReaction could never separate 'a decision delay' from 'an acceleration ramp': v1 does not have the second one.

measured.note: Not a new measurement. This record CONSUMES pace.homeToFirst and states what it does and does not determine.

kidSprintSpeed.theSecondConstraint: Published peak sprint velocity for 7-9 year olds runs about 5.0-5.8 m/s (16.4-19.0 ft/s). 18 ft/s = 5.49 m/s is the middle of it, and that is what fixes the top speed. The ACCELERATION is then solved, not chosen: for constant acceleration to a capped speed, covering d takes T/2 + d/V with T = V/a, so T = 2*(4.200 - 60/V) has no freedom left in it. It comes out at 1.7361s, an acceleration of 10.372 ft/s², and top speed reached 15.63ft down the line.
kidSprintSpeed.oneAssumptionStated: Every kid takes the SAME time to get going; a faster kid simply ends up faster. Stated rather than buried, because the alternative -- solving each stat against the same 4.200s -- would make every kid on the roster run the leg in exactly 4.2s and delete the stat.

ours.constant: src/v2/sim/params.ts RUN.TOP_SPEED_MIN_MPH, RUN.TOP_SPEED_MAX_MPH, RUN.HOME_TO_FIRST_SEC; src/v2/sim/athletes.ts sprintTopSpeedFts, sprintAccelFtS2, sprintTimeSec

drift.note: The anchored kid runs the leg in 4200ms, which is the median of the three samples exactly. That is not a coincidence and not a fit: the acceleration was solved from it. What is NOT circular, and is what makes this conformed rather than tautological, is the SECOND number the solve produces -- 10.372 ft/s² over 1.736s, which is a plausible child and was free to come out absurd. It did not.

kidSprintSpeed.spreadNote: The roster spread is 1.38x fastest-to-slowest, narrower than v1's ±6%/point (1.71x). Neither is measured. pace.homeToFirst's own driftCaveats say '4200ms is a BB runner, not the average BB runner, so the stat spread around this anchor is still unvalidated' -- that caveat is inherited whole.
kidSprintSpeed.whatWouldClose: Peak-velocity readings, not leg times, from four-to-eight-year-olds -- a 20m timing-gate split is enough to separate top speed from acceleration, which one 60ft total never can. That would replace the published second constraint with a measurement of the actual population and leave the anchor doing what it does now.

fielderRunnerParity.what: That a fielder and a baserunner are the same child, enforced structurally rather than asserted.
fielderRunnerParity.why: ★ THE MOST EXPENSIVE TUNING BUG THIS PROJECT HAS HAD, made impossible instead of forbidden. defense.fielderSpeed's history: FIELDER_SPEED sat at 210 px/s through FIVE consecutive runner slowdowns, drifting 1.20x -> 2.47x one retune at a time, and the 2026-07-24 retune then scaled BOTH by 1/1.987 and preserved 2.48x exactly. Its conclusion was 'a kid does not get faster by putting a glove on', and in v1 that is an INVARIANT A TEST ASSERTS about two constants that remain free to move.
fielderRunnerParity.theStructure: There is no fielder speed. src/v2/sim/athletes.ts has exactly one function per physical quantity, and makeFielder and makeRunner both call sprintTopSpeedFts / sprintAccelFtS2. A second constant cannot drift from the first because there is no second constant.
fielderRunnerParity.enforcement: scripts/v2/purity.lint.test.js, '★ there is exactly ONE kid speed in the sim'. Two halves, because either alone can be routed around: a TEXTUAL rule that no file but athletes.ts may read a raw physical band (TOP_SPEED_*, THROW_SPEED_*, REACTION_*, REACH_FT, HOME_TO_FIRST_SEC, ANCHOR_SPEED_STAT), and a FUNCTIONAL one that makeFielder and makeRunner agree for all 30 kids AND across stats 1-10 -- the whole range, because the drift being guarded against is in the SLOPE as much as the level, and a roster with no speed-1 kid cannot see a broken bottom end.
fielderRunnerParity.alsoCollapsed: v1 carries a SECOND, smaller version of the same drift one level down: liveplay.ts statSpeedMult gives a fielder ±5% per stat point (line 803) while a runner gets ±6% (line 360). Same class of bug, never noticed, and gone here for the same structural reason.
fielderRunnerParity.whyNotMeasurable: Nothing about this claim can be read off BB2001 footage: it is a statement about how our own code is organised. reference: 'derived' is the honest value, and the record claims nothing about BB.

catchRadius.what: How far a fielder can reach for a ball -- and how much ground that lets one child cover.
catchRadius.why: ★ THERE WAS NO RECORD FOR THIS ANYWHERE, in a defense block whose own note says its constants 'are the values most likely to need feel iteration'. v1's LIVE.CATCH_RADIUS is 34px. At v1's own 2.99398 px/ft that is 11.356 ft: a four-foot child catching a ball eleven feet away. PICKUP_RADIUS is 9.352ft and a dive adds 30px for a 21.376ft diving catch. Area goes as r², so a v1 fielder covers 14.33x the ground a real kid can, and a diving one 21.59x. defense.fielderSpeed.notSufficient spends its entire argument on chase speed and concludes 'every ball a fielder reaches is still a putout at first' -- without ever asking how cheap REACHING had been made.

measured.basis: A four-foot child's arm span is about their height, so half a span is 2ft from the body centre; a glove adds roughly another foot. Three feet is a kid at full stretch, which is what a catch radius is supposed to mean.

drift.note: known-drift against v1, not against a measurement. The two games are not being reconciled -- v1 stays as it is -- but the SIZE of the gap is pinned so it cannot be quietly reintroduced.

ours.constant: src/v2/sim/params.ts DEFENSE.REACH_FT, DEFENSE.CATCH_CENTRE_FT, DEFENSE.DIVE_REACH_FT; src/v2/sim/athletes.ts reachFt

catchRadius.theHardFloor: 3ft is not free to shrink. BOUNCE.BALL_SETTLE_MARGIN_FT lets a ball rest 1ft from the wall while FIELD_MARGIN clamps a FIELDER at 4ft, so a ball against the fence sits exactly 3ft from the nearest legal standing spot. bounce.test.ts has asserted that gap is at most 3 since PR 3, with the literal message 'PR 5 catch radius must cover this'; runners.test.ts now asserts the other end. It holds with nothing to spare, which is why it is pinned from both sides.
catchRadius.theEnvelopeIsNotASphere: ★ AND MAKING IT ONE BROKE THE INFIELD, which is the most useful thing in this record. A sphere of radius 3ft centred on a kid's chest gives a ball lying ON THE GROUND a horizontal reach of sqrt(3² - 2.88²) = 0.84ft -- the fielder has to stand almost exactly on top of a grounder to pick it up. Every routine grounder turned into a chase to the outfield wall while the election insisted the shortstop had cut it off. He had; he could not bend over. So: below chest height the reach is CYLINDRICAL (crouch and extend), above it spherical about the chest (an arm sweeping overhead). The ceiling is unchanged at 6ft.
catchRadius.whatItReplaces: v1 has no catch HEIGHT at all: its fly-ball test is dist(chaser.pos, b.pos) in the flat plane, so a fielder standing under a ball forty feet up is 'within 34px' of it. What stops that catch is LIVE.CATCHABLE_TAIL -- a rule that only the last 40% of a flight is catchable -- which is a timing constant standing in for a geometry fact. With a centre and a radius the rule falls out and the constant is not needed.
catchRadius.consequenceMeasured: Against the shipped field and physics (fielders.test.ts, park venue, stat-5 batter, 4200ms leg): a ball into the true LF-CF gap is a HIT, where defense.fielderSpeed.notSufficient measured v1's as 'out by 897ms'. A routine grounder to short is still an OUT -- secured at 2.06s, released at 2.51s, a 1.44s throw, 3.95s against the 4.20s leg -- and a grounder hit 40% harder goes THROUGH the infield and rolls 149ft. All three are what the record wanted and none of them was reachable in v1.
catchRadius.theTagUsesTheSameReach: ★ AND SO DOES THE TAG, which deleted a second v1 constant. RUN2.TAG_RADIUS is 26px = 8.7ft at v1's own scale -- a fielder tagging a runner from nine feet away -- and it exists as a separate number only because v1 has no single place for 'how far a kid can reach'. play.ts tags at reachFt(), the same three feet, from the same arm. RUN2.SAFE_RADIUS (14px, 'a runner within this of a bag counts as standing ON it') is gone outright and not even re-derived: v2's runners are LEG-parameterised, so `isSettled(r)` IS standing on the bag. v1 needs a radius because its runners are positions on a field and it has to ask geometry a question the state already answers.
catchRadius.whatWouldClose: A measurement rather than an anatomical estimate: the horizontal distance at which four-to-eight-year-olds actually catch a thrown ball, n>=3, which is an afternoon with a tape measure. It would also settle DIVE_REACH_FT, which is currently 'about a torso' and nothing better.

throwSpeed.what: How hard a kid throws, and therefore how far -- the term defense.fielderSpeed.nextLever names as binding on a batter-to-first race.
throwSpeed.why: ★ THE BB2001 MEASUREMENT IS BLOCKED AND v2 CANNOT UNBLOCK IT. defense.throwSpeed's own note: 'THE CLEANEST TARGET DOES NOT EXIST IN THIS CAPTURE' -- the contested catcher-to-second steal it planned to measure never happens, because both steals in the footage are uncontested. So this record anchors on a DIFFERENT REFERENCE CLASS, which is what reference: 'baseball' is for: published youth throwing velocity, ~36-42 mph at 8U and 37-50 at 9U.

partialReading.ageNote: 8U and 9U coaching and showcase aggregates. Our roster is four to eight, BELOW the floor, so our 30-48 band is that data extrapolated DOWN -- the same move sim.batSpeed makes and for the same reason, and it is recorded rather than hidden.
partialReading.source: Youth pitching/throwing velocity benchmarks by age.

throwSpeed.comparisonForm: throw speed / runner speed, dimensionless, which is the form defense.throwSpeed asks for and the only one that survives v1 being px/s and v2 being ft/s. Reads as: 'a throw travels N times as fast as a kid runs.'
throwSpeed.theOrdering: Ours is 2.44x-3.91x against the anchored 18.007 ft/s runner. The published band in the same units is 2.93x-4.07x. v1 KID -- the mode that actually produces base hits -- is 4.60x, just above our top. v1 CLASSIC is 9.65x, two and a half times it. That ordering is the strongest thing the blocked record can be given, and it turns KID's playability from a coincidence into a result.
throwSpeed.theRelayBecomesAConsequence: ★ AND THIS IS THE POINT. v1 had to INVENT LIVE.RELAY and gate it on a hand-picked 1.39 basepath legs, because 'throw DISTANCE provably cannot do this job: a coin-flip on a routine grounder needs an 806px throw and the longest that exists is 418px'. Here an arm has a range. Centre field to first base is 129.7ft and an average kid's maximum is 96.5ft, so 27 of 30 kids simply cannot make that throw; every one of the 30 can make the 68.2ft throw from short. A cutoff man stops being a mechanic and becomes what happens when nobody can reach the bag.
throwSpeed.vacuumCaveat: The range is a VACUUM solve -- sin(2θ) = Rg/v², taking the fast root -- while everything the BALL does is integrated with drag and Magnus. Solving a release elevation against drag needs the iteration releasePitch runs, and a throw happens far more often than a pitch. The error is OPTIMISTIC (a vacuum range overstates a real one), so maxThrowFt reads as an upper bound on what an arm can do, and the relay above is if anything under-triggered.
throwSpeed.armIsThePitchingStat: There is no separate arm stat: data/types.ts has contact/power/speed/pitching/fielding, and v1 maps arm = stats.pitching too (though only for WILDNESS -- in v1 a better arm throws straighter, never harder). Consequence worth stating: lineup.ts autoAssign puts the best arm on the mound, so outfield arms are middling by construction and the relay is the normal case rather than the exception.
throwSpeed.comparedWithThePitch: sim.pitchCorridorV2 solves a pitch to a measured FLIGHT TIME and produces a 33.5 mph release at stat 5, against 38 mph here for a max-effort throw by the same arm. Those are consistent -- a game-pace pitch to a four-year-old is not a max-effort throw -- but the pitch solve also SATURATES: at a 2.4ft aim the slowest reachable flight is ~1.14s, so ARM_MULT_MIN/MAX request flights it cannot deliver and stat 1 and stat 10 end up 78ms apart and not in the order wantSec asks for. Recorded here because it is the same arm; it belongs to sim.pitchCorridorV2 to fix.
throwSpeed.whatWouldWork: Unchanged from defense.throwSpeed: the infield-throw family, plays 03/04/12/13/15/17, located via BB's yellow throw-lane affordance, one 33ms sheet on the bracket. Failing that, a radar gun at a tee-ball practice, n>=3, which would measure the population this game is actually for.

fielderReaction.what: How long a fielder stands still before doing anything -- reading the ball, and then gathering and releasing a throw.
fielderReaction.why: v1 spends cpuReactionMs 835 + cpuThrowDelayMs 1192 = 2027ms of a fielder standing perfectly still, 48% of the batter's entire 4200ms leg, and defense.fielderSpeed.nextLever identifies that fixed overhead plus the throw -- not the chase -- as what actually decides the race.

partialReading.why: Simple visual reaction time in 8-10 year olds. A fielder must also decide WHERE the ball is going, so our band starts above it at 300-500ms.

fielderReaction.theConfoundIsGone: defense.cpuReaction refused to promote its own 1050ms partial reading (n=5) for a DEFINITIONAL reason, quoted whole: 'a displacement threshold cannot separate a DECISION DELAY from an ACCELERATION RAMP. Our cpuReactionMs is a deliberate AI pause; if BB's fielders instead start immediately and accelerate slowly, the same 1050ms would be measuring something we do not model.' v2 MODELS THE RAMP (sim.kidSprintSpeed), so the two are no longer confounded and that record's open question changes shape: a future measurement of BB can now be compared against reaction + ramp rather than against a single number standing for both.

ours.constant: src/v2/sim/params.ts DEFENSE.REACTION_MIN_SEC, DEFENSE.REACTION_MAX_SEC, DEFENSE.RELEASE_SEC; src/v2/sim/athletes.ts reactionSec

fielderReaction.itIsAlsoPartOfTheElection: ★ A SECOND FINDING, and it was a real bug first. The chaser election ranks fielders on when they can cut the ball off, and the first version computed that as pure travel time -- for a fielder who has not seen the ball yet and is not moving. It elected a shortstop whose cut-off was 1.42s away when 0.46s of that would be spent standing still; the ball went past him at 7ft and he trailed it eighty feet into left field before catching up with it at rest. The read is now part of the journey. Nothing about this is visible in a fielder's POSITION, which is why it could only be found by running the election against the pursuit it was predicting.
fielderReaction.whatWouldWork: defense.cpuReaction's own plan, now with a second thing to look for: read first-motion frames at >=2x magnification on a clockFidelity-gated capture, but ALSO read the fielder's speed profile over the following second. A ramp and a pause look identical at one frame and completely different over thirty.

chaserElectionGate.what: Whether expressing v1's cut-ahead gate as a RATIO rather than a fixed duration actually fixes what defense.chaserElection says is wrong with it.
chaserElectionGate.finding: ★ IT DOES NOT, AND THE PR THAT MADE THE CHANGE ASSERTED THAT IT DID. defense.chaserElection.stabilityClaimCorrected reads: 'CUT_AHEAD_MS is a fixed ms gate compared against BALL-PATH times returned by cutOff(). Slowing fielders pushes every interception later along the path, so the gaps between candidates inflate while the gate does not -- it gets relatively cheaper to clear and the zone owner is overridden more often. It cannot be speed-neutral by construction.' The obvious inference is that a dimensionless gate would be. It is not.

measured.grid: Ground balls, spray -42..+42 in 2deg steps x exit velocity 40/55/70/85/100 ft/s, park venue, the autoAssign lineup, reaction zeroed so only the gate varies.

chaserElectionGate.why: Both gate forms drift by the same 7.4 percentage points across a 4x spread of defence speed. The override rate moves because a speed change alters WHICH FIELDERS CAN INTERCEPT THE BALL AT ALL -- a slow fielder's cutOff returns null and they drop out of the comparison entirely -- and no gate form touches that. The gate is not the dominant term.
chaserElectionGate.whatThisCorrects: defense.chaserElection's diagnosis is a correct observation with an incomplete mechanism. Its MEASUREMENT (27.7% -> 32.4% over a 2.48x speed change) stands and is not challenged here; what this shows is that the fixed gate is not what produced it, so re-deriving CUT_AHEAD_MS at the new speed -- the work that record schedules -- would not have stabilised the rate either.
chaserElectionGate.whyKeepTheRatioAnyway: A smaller and honest reason. It is dimensionless, so it cannot silently become a different rule when the times it compares change scale, and there is no unit for a future retune to leave stale -- which is the failure mode that produced v1's 400ms sitting unexamined through five speed changes. A correctness-of-form change, not a measured improvement.
chaserElectionGate.whatWouldClose: The interesting question this opens is whether an election that ranks on cut-off time is stable under ANY gate, or whether the two-regime structure itself needs a term for 'nobody can head it off'. That is answerable with the same sweep and a third gate form, and it belongs with the play reducer rather than here.

gapBallOutcome.what: What actually happens to the six plays defense.fielderSpeed.notSufficient measured in v1 -- run through a real play reducer rather than a test harness that admitted its own bias.
gapBallOutcome.why: ★ THIS IS THE CLAIM v2 WAS BUILT TO TEST. defense.fielderSpeed.notSufficient measured six balls in v1 and every one was an out at first, including a ball into the true LF-CF gap (out by 897ms). Its conclusion was that the cause was structural -- 'our outfield is too shallow relative to the diamond... any real fix to offense has to touch geometry.FIELD_POSITIONS or the throw ratio, not the chase'. PR 5 answered it with a test-only harness that stepped ONE chaser against ONE runner and said so in its own header: 'no relays, no cutoff, no CPU baserunning policy, no errors. Every one of those omissions makes the DEFENCE look better than it will be, so a hit here is a lower bound on a hit.' This is the same six plays through the thing that plays the game.

measured.defence: systems/lineup.ts autoAssign over ROSTER[0..8] -- the SHIPPED planner, not a hand-picked nine

gradient.what: Grounders swept over 15 spray angles at three contact qualities. Hits, out of 15.

gapBallOutcome.theGradientIsTheResult: A soft grounder is an out almost anywhere, a medium one finds the holes, a hard one gets through -- and NOTHING WAS TUNED TO PRODUCE IT. v1 measured every ball a fielder reached as an out, at every angle and every contact quality, which is a defence with no gradient at all.
gapBallOutcome.notABabipClaim: ★ AND THIS IS NOT BABIP, which matters because the number is tempting. The sweep is grounders only: no fly balls, no strikeouts, no walks, one batter, one venue, and the sprays are uniform rather than distributed the way real contact is. PR 8's harness is what measures BABIP, over plate appearances rather than launch specs. Reading 12/15 as a batting average is exactly the overclaim pace.pitchCorridor exists to warn about.
gapBallOutcome.theArmAtShort: ★ A FINDING WORTH MORE THAN THE HEADLINE: the routine grounder to short is now a SINGLE, and the reason is the arm. systems/lineup.ts autoAssign scores shortstop on `fielding*2 + speed` and never looks at `pitching`, so this nine puts a 34mph arm (max range 77ft) at the position with the longest routine throw in the infield. He fields the ball at 72ft and cannot quite beat the runner across. The same ball hit to the second-base side, where the throw is 40ft, is an out. v1 could not surface this because its throws were 9.65x runner speed and its catch radius was 11.4ft -- arm strength never bound anything. NOT FIXED HERE: autoAssign is v1 code and v1 must stay byte-identical; v2's own lineup planner is PR 7's.
bugsThisFound: The election treated a ball skipping through the infield as IN THE AIR (phase === flight between hops), so it sent whoever was nearest the next bounce. The pitcher fielded a grounder forty feet behind the shortstop. Fixed by splitting the regimes on APEX HEIGHT against the same ceiling `canReach` enforces.

The election charged every fielder a fresh STANDING-START ramp on each re-read, saying a running kid was up to 0.87s slower than he was. The shortstop would not CHARGE: told he could not reach the ball out in front, he settled for meeting it where it happened to arrive, fourteen feet deeper. Fixed by `sprintTimeForFt(..., fromFts)`. Worth 7 of 15 outs on the soft-grounder sweep on its own.

`shouldSwitch` was handed a null incumbent score, so its third guard could not run and every challenger won. A grounder's single `land` event then fell inside the switch cooldown, so the first guess -- made in the air regime -- became permanent.

`startLeg` has no occupancy check (it is handed one runner and cannot see the traffic), and the reducer did not add one, so two runners settled on the same base. That does not look like a baserunning bug: it looks like a runner VANISHING, because finishPlay writes one baseIds entry. Caught only by the accounting sweep.
gapBallOutcome.reMeasuredAt: 2026-08-01 (PR 7). Two changes moved these numbers and both are recorded rather than absorbed: play.ts now asks `isFair` (until PR 7 every batted ball in v2 was fair, so the foul ball did not exist), and the defence RE-READS the ball without RE-TRACING it -- the trajectory does not change between ticks, so re-computing the prediction produced an identical answer at the price of two thousand RK4 steps. The six named plays are unchanged; the gradient moved 3/12/13 to 2/10/14 and the relay rate 16% to 14%.
gapBallOutcome.whatWouldClose: Nothing -- this one is measured and conformed. What it hands forward is PR 8's job: the same defence over 50k plate appearances, where BABIP, the launch-angle split and the exit-velocity shape can be compared against real baseball bands instead of six named plays.

playClock.what: The hard cap on a play, and the assertion v1 never had: that no legitimate play reaches it.
playClock.why: ★ A CAP THAT FIRES IS A SOFT-LOCK THAT WAS CAUGHT, NOT A RULE. v1's LIVE.MAX_PLAY_MS is 21862 and its own comment says 'NOT measured -- scaled with RUNNER_SPEED'. Nothing in v1 asserts a legitimate play stays under it, so the cap quietly became the way some plays ended: eight separate anti-hang guards elsewhere in liveplay.ts exist because plays wedged, and each was added after the fact. The cap is only a backstop if something proves it is never the mechanism.

measured.grid: 3 venues x 12 spray angles x 5 contact qualities (35-120 ft/s, -3 to 30 deg), two runners aboard.

playClock.theBound: The longest legitimate sequence is a ball to the deepest fence, a chase, a relay in, and a runner going first to home: 180ft from a standing start is ~11s at the slowest stat. Twenty seconds clears the measured worst case (12.38s) by 38%.
playClock.andTheGuardsAreFewer: v2 needs fewer anti-hang guards than v1 because two of v1's exist to undo bad geometry rather than to stop a hang: `wildSettlePoint` rotates rather than truncates an overshoot 'because a fielder then presses against the clamp boundary until MAX_PLAY_MS', and `settleBallAt` clamps every settle site for the same reason. v2 inherits the second (bounce.ts owns it) and does not need the first, because a throw that misses is simply live at the bag rather than sailing to an unreachable spot.
playClock.whatWouldClose: Re-run the sweep after PR 7 adds tag-ups, rundowns and steals -- each of which lengthens a play, and rundowns most of all. The assertion is the thing to keep, not the number.

cutoffRelay.what: Whether the cutoff relay emerges from arm range on its own, and whether v1's look-back concession was needed to make it work.
cutoffRelay.why: ★ v1 HAD TO INVENT THE RELAY, and says so: 'throw DISTANCE provably cannot do this job. A coin-flip on a routine grounder would need an 806px throw to first; the longest that exists anywhere is 418px.' So LIVE.RELAY is a MECHANIC, armed by a hand-picked depth of 1.39 basepath legs and gated on CPU-defence-and-CLASSIC-only. Here an arm has a range: centre field to first base is 129.7ft and 27 of 30 kids cannot throw it, so a cutoff man is what happens when nobody can reach the bag.
cutoffRelay.theLookBackRuleWasNotNeeded: ★ v1's RelayState.committed is a CONCESSION -- the defence stops playing for the one leg a runner is already on -- and its comment is emphatic that 'without this the relay buys nothing. The ball lands back on the mound at ~4470ms, bestBeatableBase sees the batter running to second, and MOUND->SECOND is 118px (286ms) against a 4197ms leg, so the pitcher guns him down every single time and a gap ball is still just a single.' That is a statement about v1's GEOMETRY, not about relays. Here the same bestBeatableBase veto is the whole policy and the concession is absent: gap balls come out as doubles, not as singles and not as outs. Omitting it was the deliberate test, and the outcome is in sim.gapBallOutcome.
cutoffRelay.invariantsKept: Three of v1's, each of which was a bug first. ThrowTarget stays a discriminated union so a relay leg and a throw at a bag cannot be confused; the `kind: 'fielder'` branch RETURNS BEFORE THE RUNNER LOOP, which is what makes an out on a relay structurally impossible ('do not restructure it away'); and PLAY.RELAY_MAX_LEGS caps the chain. A test steps every relay in a sweep and asserts the outs count does not move on the tick a relay leg lands.
cutoffRelay.whatWouldClose: Nothing here. The open question it hands PR 8 is whether 14% is the right rate -- it is a consequence of the arm band (sim.throwSpeed, still awaiting-measurement) and would move with it.

strikeZone.what: Where a strike is, in feet.
strikeZone.why: ★ THE THIRD v1 CONSTANT WITH NO UNITS, AND THE PUREST OF THE THREE. LIVE.CATCH_RADIUS was 34 PIXELS, which converts to a wrong number of feet (11.36). RUN2.TAG_RADIUS was 26px, likewise (8.7ft). v1's PLATE_ZONE is { W: 96, H: 100 } in 'plate coords' -- a space art/plateView.ts maps to the screen at about 1.8x and which NOTHING RELATES TO THE FIELD. It is not a wrong size; it has no size. v1 never needed the zone to be a place, only a rectangle to test a rolled crossing point against, so the question never came up. v2's crossing is a fact about an integrated trajectory, so the zone has to be somewhere real.
strikeZone.derivation: WIDTH: Official Baseball Rules 2.02 and Little League Rulebook 1.05 both specify a 17-inch plate, and a strike is 'any part of the ball over any part of home plate' -- so the BALL'S CENTRE may sit a radius outside each edge. Half-width is 8.5in + r_ball, computed by zoneHalfWidthFt() rather than restated. HEIGHT: the rulebook defines the zone ON THE BATTER, from the hollow beneath the kneecap to the midpoint between the shoulders and the belt. Anthropometric knee height is about 0.28 of stature and the sternal notch about 0.62, so the band is a FRACTION of height and a taller kid has a taller zone.
strikeZone.confidenceExemption: n=1 with high confidence, which the schema allows for reference: 'physics' and by extension a rulebook -- a rule is not a sample. The price of the exemption is naming the source, and both rulebook sections are named above.

ours.constant: src/v2/sim/params.ts ATBAT.PLATE_HALF_WIDTH_IN, ATBAT.ZONE_BOTTOM_FRAC, ATBAT.ZONE_TOP_FRAC; src/v2/sim/athletes.ts zoneHalfWidthFt, zoneBandFt

strikeZone.theUmpireAsksTheTRAJECTORY: v1's pitchkind.ts sets `inZone` on an aim point plus a scatter roll -- a number invented at release, before the ball has gone anywhere. v2's flyToPlate integrates the ball through drag and Magnus and reports where it actually was when z reached zero, and isStrike looks at that. A curveball that breaks out of the zone is a ball BECAUSE IT BROKE.
strikeZone.whatWouldClose: Nothing. This is a rulebook measurement plus two anthropometric fractions, and the fractions are the only soft part -- a real 4-8-year-old's knee and sternum heights, n>=3, would replace them with a measurement of the population the game is for.

plateDiscipline.what: How a batter decides to swing, and how well he times it -- which turn out to be the same question asked twice.
plateDiscipline.why: ★ ONE ERROR, TWO BEHAVIOURS. The obvious build gives a batter a chase rate and a whiff rate and tunes them apart; v1 does exactly that, with five constants in resolveCpuPitch (ball chance 0/0.1/0.45/0.85 per band, chase 0.2, and a swing band rolled off the contact stat) that describe an outcome distribution rather than a kid. But a hitter does not have two faculties. Give him ONE judgement error, sized by his contact stat, and both fall out: he swings when he BELIEVES the pitch is a strike, so chases and takes are consequences; and the same error in time becomes SwingSpec.timingErrorSec, so whiffs and weak contact come out of the window contact.ts already grades against. A better-contact kid then chases less AND times better, from one number.

partialReading.why: NOTHING MEASURES THIS, and that is still the honest status AFTER PR 8's harness ran. The harness measured OURS -- over 50,045 plate appearances, and those numbers are in `ours` -- but the record's reference class was never our own output. A chase rate has no on-screen representation in BB2001 any more than a swing window does (see pace.swingWindows, a permanent `note` for exactly this reason), and real-baseball plate-discipline data is for adults facing 90mph. So `measured` stays null: the record pins our value and claims nothing about anyone else's, which is what `awaiting-measurement` means.

plateDiscipline.theBoundedNoiseFailedSilently: Rng.bell is the Irwin-Hall sum of three uniforms -- bit-stable, `+` and `/` only, and the answer to the `normal()` gap rng.ts documents. Its support is BOUNDED at ±3 sigma, which is a feature (a batter who misjudges by six sigma is not a batter) and a trap. At the first draft's 0.115/0.035 a swinging strike needed 2.5 sigma, and the measurement over 4,000 pitches was ZERO swinging strikes at EVERY contact stat -- not rare, none. A game in which nobody can swing through a pitch is a missing mechanic rather than a bad tuning, and a bounded noise turns that from unlikely into impossible without saying so. The band is now sized AGAINST BAT.CONTACT_WINDOW_FRAC and a test asserts the relationship rather than the values.
plateDiscipline.aFractionNeverMilliseconds: The temporal half is a fraction of the pitch's flight. pace.swingWindows records what absolute windows cost: v1's 380ms CONTACT band sat over a 270ms flight, so 'a tap at the instant of release still connects, and timing stops being a skill'. BAT.CONTACT_WINDOW_FRAC is scale-free for that reason; a batter noise in milliseconds would reintroduce the same failure from the other side, and the two would drift apart the next time the pitch corridor is re-measured.

ours.constant: src/v2/sim/params.ts ATBAT.JUDGE_FT_WORST/BEST, ATBAT.JUDGE_FRAC_WORST/BEST, ATBAT.TWO_STRIKE_PROTECT_FT; src/v2/sim/athletes.ts plateJudgementFt, swingTimingSigmaFrac
ours.over: 878 games / 50,004 plate appearances / 254,128 pitches, 8 seeds x 3 venues, all 30 kids

plateDiscipline.twoStrikeProtection: Without it a batter offers only at what he READS as a strike, so every misread with two strikes is a called third -- which turns a poor-contact kid into a strikeout machine rather than the foul-ball machine a six-year-old actually is. It is what balances strikeouts against fouls, and PR 8's harness measured it rather than leaving it a claim: 68.3% of two-strike pitches are swung at, against a 55.7% swing rate over all pitches. NOTE it is currently balancing toward BOTH at once -- 43.0% strikeouts AND 3.4 fouls per fair ball (sim.battedBallSplit). PR 9.
plateDiscipline.whatWouldClose: PR 8's harness has now run, and it closed the OURS column, not the record: K%, BB% and the swing/take split are measured over 50,045 plate appearances and pinned in harness.test.ts. What remains missing is the thing that was always missing -- published plate-discipline rates for four-to-eight-year-olds. Nothing found so far starts below 9U. The same afternoon of tee-ball observation that would close sim.batSpeed would go a long way here too, since K and BB are countable from a scorebook without any instrument at all.
plateDiscipline.whatTheHARNESSEXPOSED: ★ THE STRIKEOUT RATE IS 43.0%, AND IT WAS 20.6% BEFORE sim.contactGeometry WAS FIXED. The difference is not a regression -- the old number was arithmetic over a defect, because 30% of the balls it counted in play were swings that had actually missed the ball and were being clamped into vertical pop-ups. 43% is what this model has always meant; it is only now visible. Nearly half of all plate appearances ending in a strikeout is wrong for four-to-eight-year-olds by any reading, and the constant it lands on is named: ATBAT.UNDERCUT_FROM_JUDGE (0.45) turns a vertical READ error into a bat PLACEMENT error at nearly half strength, against a barrel that forgives 2.70 inches. Real batters place the bat far better than they judge the zone, because they track the ball all the way in. That is a tuning constant. PR 8 did not touch it, and PR 9 -- which was scoped to own it -- MEASURED THE REASON NOT TO: sweeping it to a 15% strikeout rate takes runs per game from 4.9 to 15.4, because 43% strikeouts is currently hiding a defence that converts under a third of balls in play. It moves in PR 10, alongside the defence. See sim.retuneTargets.
plateDiscipline.theProtectionCurveIsNotMonotonic: ★ A PR 9 FINDING, AND IT CORRECTS THIS RECORD'S OWN twoStrikeProtection PARAGRAPH. That paragraph argues protection exists because 'a batter who only ever swings at what he READS as a strike takes a third strike every time his read is wrong'. Measured over 80 games per point, K% against ATBAT.TWO_STRIKE_PROTECT_FT runs 44.4 / 40.4 / 42.5 / 45.1 / 47.4 for 0 / 0.25 / 0.55 / 0.9 / 1.5. The mechanism is REAL -- going from no protection to some does cut strikeouts, 44.4 to 40.4 -- but the curve TURNS, because past the minimum the extra protective swings whiff (24-26%) more often than the takes they replace get called for strike three. Our shipped 0.55 is on the WRONG SIDE of its own optimum. ★ NOT MOVED IN PR 9: it is one of the three constants sim.retuneTargets defers, and 0.25 also takes the walk rate to 17.1% -- outside the 8-14 target -- so it cannot be set alone either. PR 10, with the defence. What PR 9 owed it was the measurement, and a test that asserts protection against the two-strike SWING rate (which is monotonic) rather than the strikeout rate (which is not).

foulBalls.what: That a batted ball can be foul at all.
foulBalls.why: ★ UNTIL PR 7, EVERY BATTED BALL IN v2 WAS FAIR. field.ts has exported isFair since it was written and NOTHING CALLED IT -- play.ts stepped a ball, caromed it, relayed it and settled it without ever asking which side of the line it came down on. contact.ts emits a foulTip that nothing consumed. The foul ball is roughly a third of the pitches in a real plate appearance and a fifth of a batter's outcomes, and it did not exist.
foulBalls.theRuleIsTHESHORTVERSION: Fair or foul is decided WHERE THE BALL FIRST TOUCHES DOWN. Real baseball's rule is longer -- a ball that lands foul BEFORE first or third and then rolls fair is fair, which is what makes a bunt down the line a real play -- and this is deliberately the short version, recorded rather than pretended away. What it cannot be is absent.
foulBalls.andOverTheFENCE: A ball hooked over the pole side is a foul, not a home run. play.ts asks isFair at the exit point too; before PR 7 it called every ball that cleared the wall a home run regardless of where it left.
foulBalls.whatItMoved: The PR 6 records were measured on a reducer in which every ball was fair, so they were re-run: the six named plays are unchanged (their sprays are all fair), the BABIP gradient moved 3/12/13 to 2/10/14 and the relay rate 16% to 14%. Both of those moved mostly for a different reason -- the defence now re-READS the ball without re-TRACING it -- and the records say so.

ours.constant: src/v2/sim/play.ts (isFair at first touchdown and at the fence)

foulBalls.whatWouldClose: The long rule, if a bunt ever matters: a ball landing foul inside the bases is fair once it rolls past one. It needs a base-line crossing test rather than a single point sample, and nothing in the game asks for it yet.

gameShape.what: What a whole v2 game actually produces, reported and NOT conformed.
gameShape.why: ★ THIS RECORD EXISTS TO BE READ, NOT TO BE MET. It is the first time v2 has been able to say anything about a game rather than a play, and the temptation is to compare the numbers to baseball's and start tuning. Two reasons not to. First, PR 8's harness is what measures these properly -- over 50,000 plate appearances across seeded runs, not 1,166.
